title: What is known about 1RB1LC_1LC0RF_0LF1LD_0LE---_1RF1LC_1LE0RA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LC_1LC0RF_0LF1LD_0LE---_1RF1LC_1LE0RA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and looks hard. The run is a sequence of phases. A phase starts with a block of l cells, mostly ones, followed by a short tail; rounds turn the ones into words 110, four ones for two words (proved in Lean for any size), and at the end of the phase the block is about 3l/2 long. Jumping over the rounds with the Lean rule, the run is followed exactly through 47 phases, to about 3.4·1018 steps and a block of 2.39·109 cells, without a halt; the tail is always one of five, and on them the phase map is an exact 3/2 map whose parities steer the tail. The tail's own block of ones is processed like a small copy of the main run, so the tails that can arise are not a finite family: a reduction to a halting condition on the map stops there.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 41,313 cells have been visited and 21,863 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: One round, and a phase of rounds by induction
claims.text: From 0^inf F> 0 0 (110)^x 1^(y+5) R the machine reaches 0^inf F> 0 0 (110)^(x+2) 1^(y+1) R in 12x+26 steps, for all x, y and every tape R; k rounds take (110)^x 1^(y+4k+1) to (110)^(x+2k) 1^(y+1).

claims.title: The phase map with an empty tail
claims.text: A phase starts with the head in C on a new cell at the left end and l cells (1^l or 10 1^(l-2)) before the tail. On the run from blank tape and on constructed tapes: with an empty tail, an even l goes to 3l/2 + 4 with an empty tail and an odd l to (3l+5)/2 with the tail 011; with the tail (011)^c an even l goes to 3l/2 + 4 + 3c with an empty tail.

claims.title: 17 phases of the run, exactly
claims.text: From blank tape the phase lengths are 88, 136, 208, 316, 478, 721, 1,084, 1,633, 2,452, 3,685, 5,530, 8,302, 12,457, 18,688, 28,039, 42,061, 63,091 (step 2.4·109). The tail is empty or 011 until 42,061, the first odd l with a non-empty tail; it leaves the tail 011111111011.

claims.title: 47 phases, 3.4·10<sup>18</sup> steps, without a halt
claims.text: c/m6fast.c runs the machine but replaces each stretch of rounds 0^inf F> 0 0 (110)^x 1^y R (y ≥ 5) by its result from the Lean rule rounds, with the exact step count. From blank tape it reaches 47 phase starts, the last at step 3,428,480,554,246,233,263 with l = 2,390,425,546, without a halt (3 minutes, 3 GB of tape). Its first 17 phases agree with c/m6phase.c. The tails met are only [], [2], [8,2], [26,2] and [359,2] (a list [b1,b2,...] stands for 0 1^b1 0 1^b2 ...).

claims.title: The phase map on these tails
claims.text:
For large l (measured at l = 105 to 105+3) the next length and tail are:
taill evenl odd
empty3l/2 + 4, empty(3l+5)/2, [2]
[2]3l/2 + 7, empty(3l−1)/2, [8,2]
[8,2]3l/2 + 19, empty(3l−19)/2, [26,2]
[26,2]3l/2 + 46, empty(3l−625)/2, [359,2]
[359,2]3l/2 + 538, [8,2](3l−1717)/2, [1232,2]
[1232,2]3l/2 + 1855, empty(3l−3079)/2, [2780,2]
The 47 phases of the run follow this table exactly. For a tail [b,2] the constants are not a simple function of b: the block 1^b is itself worked through like a small run (for instance tail [5534,2], odd l, leaves [18692,2], and [18692,2] leaves [42065,2], near the main run's lengths 5530, 18688, 42061), and some b leave longer tails such as [212987,8,2]. When b is not small against l the outputs change regime again.

claims.title: Why it is hard
claims.text: The lengths grow by a factor 3/2 a phase and their parities behave like coin flips, as in Mahler's 3/2 problem and the Antihydra cryptid. Which tails can arise, and whether one of them leads the head to D reading 1 (the only halting transition), depends on these parities.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Equivalent to: does the phase map, with its tail of digits, ever reach a phase end in which D reads 1? A reduction to a closed system (a halts-iff statement about the map) is not reached: on the five tails of the run the map is the table above, but an odd l on [359,2] leads to [1232,2] and then to an unbounded chain of tails whose blocks follow their own 3/2 dynamics, and the phase ends for general tails are not decoded or proved. No halting tail has been found.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Each phase of this machine multiplies the length of a block of ones by about 3/2, and whether the length is even or odd decides what happens to a few cells at the end of the tape. Questions of that kind, about the parities of numbers growing by 3/2, are famously out of reach.

facts.text: Followed exactly to 3.4·10<sup>18</sup> steps, jumping over the rounds with the Lean rule; block length 2.39·10<sup>9</sup>.
The rounds of a phase are proved in Lean for every size.
Growth of the block per phase, steered by parities.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.523). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 41,313 cells (32,661 left of the start, 47 right), with a density of 1s of 0.529.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: A block of ones and a tail
html: Everything happens left of the start. At the start of a phase the tape is a block of l cells, 1^l (or 10 1^(l-2)), and after it a short tail, often empty. During the phase the left part is 0 0 (110)^x 1^y: in each round the head sweeps in from the left, takes four ones and leaves two more words 110 (Lean: round, rounds). Two words of three cells for four ones of one cell: when the ones run out the block is about 3l/2 long.

sections.heading: Multiply by 3/2, watch the parity
html: With an empty tail an even l becomes 3l/2 + 4; an odd l becomes (3l+5)/2 and leaves the tail 011, which the next even phase swallows (3l/2 + 4 + 3). The phases from blank tape:
Two odd lengths in a row put a longer tail in place: at l = 42,061 the tail 011 becomes 011111111011. What tails can be built, and what they do, depends on the run of parities.

Jumping over the rounds (they are proved in Lean, so a simulator may apply them in one stroke) the run can be followed to 47 phases and 3.4·1018 steps. Only five tails occur, and on them the map is exact:

taill evenl odd
empty3l/2 + 4, empty(3l+5)/2, [2]
[2]3l/2 + 7, empty(3l−1)/2, [8,2]
[8,2]3l/2 + 19, empty(3l−19)/2, [26,2]
[26,2]3l/2 + 46, empty(3l−625)/2, [359,2]
[359,2]3l/2 + 538, [8,2](3l−1717)/2, [1232,2]
[1232,2]3l/2 + 1855, empty(3l−3079)/2, [2780,2]

([b1,b2] is the tail 0 1^b1 0 1^b2.) Each odd length on a non-empty tail lengthens the tail's block; an odd length on [359,2], which the run has not met yet, would begin a chain [1232,2], [2780,2], ... in which the tail's block behaves like a small copy of the whole run.

sections.heading: A 3/2 problem
html: The only halting transition is D reading 1. The rounds never halt (they are proved in Lean), so a halt can only come at the end of a phase, where the tail is rewritten. Whether that ever happens depends on the parities of numbers that grow by a factor 3/2 at every phase, like Mahler's 3/2 problem or the Antihydra machine: nobody knows how to predict them, and treating them as coin flips gives no reason to expect a halt soon. Each phase costs about 2.25 times the previous one, so plain simulation stops after a few more phases; skipping the rounds by their Lean rule would go much further.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

family: 3/2 Collatz-like map with a tail of digits
summary: Phases: a block of l cells becomes about 3l/2, the parity of l steering a tail of digits whose own block is processed like a small copy of the run; 47 phases (3.4·10^18 steps) without a halt. Open.
